The structure is located close to the pyramid of Pepi II, a ruler of the Sixth Dynasty. The stone quarry for the structure is located west of the Red Pyramid of Sneferu.

title: Pyramid of Pepi II
description: The Pyramid of Pepi II was the tomb of King Pepi II, located in southern Saqqara, to the northwest of the Mastabat al-Fir'aun. It was the final full pyramid complex to be built in Ancient Egypt. Long used as a quarry, the pyramid was excavated for the first time by Gaston Maspero in 1881. Its ruins were studied in exhaustive detail by Gustave Jéquier, who was able to reconstruct the funerary complex and the texts on the walls of the funerary chamber in the course of his excavation campaigns from 1932–1935. Since 1996, thorough investigations of the pyramid and its surroundings have been carried out by the Mission a.

title: Serapeum
description: The Serapeum of Saqqara was the ancient Egyptian burial place for sacred bulls of the Apis cult at Memphis. It was believed that the bulls were incarnations of the god Ptah, which would become immortal after death as Osiris-Apis, a name which evolved to Serapis (Σέραπις) in the Hellenistic period, and Userhapi (ⲟⲩⲥⲉⲣϩⲁⲡⲓ) in Coptic. It is one of the animal catacombs in the Saqqara necropolis, which also contains the burial vaults of the mother cows of the Apis, the Iseum.

title: Temple of Kalabsha
description: Kalabsha Temple, also known as Mandulis Temple, is an ancient Egyptian temple whose original location is Bab Kalabsha, about 50 km south of Aswan. The temple was located on the west bank of the Nile and was built around 30 BC during Roman rule in Egypt. It is a temple for the worship of the gods Mandulis, the Nubian god of the sun. It was created on the ruins of another temple of King Amenhotep III and was built during the reign of Emperor Augustus, but it was not completed. The dimensions of the temple are 76 meters long and 22 meters wide. Although the temple was established in the Roman era, it contains drawings of the god Horus on the inner wall of the temple. The temple contains a staircase leading to the roof, which offers an open view of the temple and the sacred lake. There are many historical records on the walls of the temple, including orders from the Roman commander Aurelius Bessarion in 250 AD, prohibiting pigs from entering the temple, as well as writings by the Nubian king Silko, in which he records his victories over Belmis and represents himself as a Roman soldier on the back of a horse. Silko was a Christian Nubian king of the Kingdom of Noubatia.

title: Temple of Beit el-Wali
description: The Temple of the Governor's House is a temple located in ancient Nubia, 55 meters south of Aswan. It is considered the oldest temple of King Ramesses II in Lower Nubia and was dedicated to the god Amun and the god Khnum and Anqet. The temple was moved in 1960 AD during the construction of the High Dam, where it was moved to a higher location than its old location near the Kalabsha Temple south of the High Dam. It was moved by Polish archaeologists and funded by the Swiss Institute and the Chicago Institute.

title: Ed Dakka Temple
description: El-Dikka is a temple located in Lower Nubia. It is a Greek-Roman temple dedicated to the worship of the ancient Egyptian god Thoth, the god of wisdom. The construction of the temple began in the third century BC by order of the Meroitic King Arkamani in cooperation with King Ptolemy IV, who added the portal. Then King Ptolemy IX expanded the temple by adding a hypostyle hall with two and perhaps three rows of columns. During the Roman rule of Egypt, Emperor Augustus and Tiberius expanded the temple by adding internal and external walls. The Temple of Dekka was transformed into a fortress during the Roman era, surrounding it with a defensive wall 270 meters long and 444 meters wide, with an entrance to the Nile.

title: Maharraqa
description: The Temple of the Holocaust is located in Lower Nubia, about 120 km from Aswan in the south direction. Several years after the Roman Empire took control of Egypt in 30 BC, the Kushites from the Kingdom of Meroe carried out raids on the First Cataract area in 23 BC. The Roman envoy to Egypt, Petronius, defeated the Meroitic raids and then stationed his forces on the southern border of his region near Qasr Ibrim. After several consultations and discussions, the borders were demarcated between the Kingdom of Meroe and Roman Egypt.  So the Muharraq Monastery was the farthest border of Roman Egypt.

title: Temple of Derr
description: The Temple of Al-Durr, or Al-Durr, is an Egyptian temple carved into the rock of Lower Nubia. It was built by Ramesses II during the rule of the Nineteenth Dynasty. It is the only temple carved in rock that was established by Ramesses II in Nubia on the right (eastern) bank of the Nile River, and its location was in the Al-Durr area. The distinct location of the temple “may be due to the fact that the river, as it approaches the Cursco bend, moves in an 'unnatural' direction towards the south-east.” The building of Al-Durr was known in ancient times as the temple of Ramesses-Meriamun, Ramesses II in the fever of Ra. It was dedicated to the god Ra-Horakhti. Scholars disagreed about the date of construction of the temple: French Egyptologist Nicolas Grimald places the date in the thirteenth year of the reign of Ramesses II, assuming that this coincided with the first jubilee of his accession to the throne. On the other hand, John Baines and Jaromir Malek believe that the Temple of Durr “was built in the second part of the king’s rule,” perhaps because “the shape of the building and its inscriptions resemble the great temple at Abu Simbel.” Abu Simbel was built between the years 24 and 31 of the reign of Ramesses. According to Joyce Tyldesley, the Temple of Al-Durr was built by Setau, who was the governor of Kush or Nubia between 38 and 63 of Ramesses' reign.

title: Edfu Temple
description: The Temple of Edfu is an Egyptian temple located on the west bank of the Nile in Edfu, Upper Egypt. The city was known in the Hellenistic period in Koine Greek as Ἀπόλλωνος πόλις and in Latin as Apollonopolis Magna, after the chief god Horus, who was identified as Apollo under the interpretatio graeca. It is one of the best preserved shrines in Egypt. The temple was built in the Ptolemaic Kingdom between 237 and 57 BC. The inscriptions on its walls provide important information on language, myth and religion during the Hellenistic period in Egypt. In particular, the Temple's inscribed building texts "provide details [both] of its construction, and also preserve information about the mythical interpretation of this and all other temples as the Island of Creation." There are also "important scenes and inscriptions of the Sacred Drama which related the age-old conflict between Horus and Seth." They are translated by the Edfu-Project.

The name of the Omar Makram Mosque in Tahrir Square has always been associated with the condolences and funerals of famous figures in Egypt.

title: Monastery of Saint Mary Deipara
description: Klasztor Syryjczyków – koptyjski klasztor, położony w Wadi an-Natrun w północnym Egipcie. Założony został w VI wieku przez trzech mnichów klasztoru Świętego Paisjusza, którzy pod wpływem doktryny monofizytyzmu opuścili macierzysty erem i założyli w pobliżu odrębny. Klasztor pełni swoją rolę aż po czasy współczesne.

title: Alexandria Center for Artistic Creativity
description: The Freedom Center for Creativity or the Alexandria Creativity Center is an Egyptian cultural center, located in the city of Alexandria. It is considered one of the first cultural centers established in the Arab Republic of Egypt. Indeed, it is the first Egyptian cultural center established in Alexandria. It is affiliated with the Cultural Development Fund, and the Ministry of Culture supervises it. Many diverse activities are held here that serve to educate children and youth who live in the city of Alexandria.

title: National Circus
description: The National Circus is a well-known theatre located in Egypt. It is a popular destination for locals and tourists alike.

title: British Council
description: The British Council is a well-known library located in Egypt. It is a popular destination for locals and tourists alike.

title: KV18
description: Tomb No. 18, known scientifically as KV18, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It was intended as a burial place for Pharaoh Ramesses

title: KV17
description: The tomb of Seti I, or tomb No. KV17 in the Valley of the Kings tombs classification, is one of the most famous and beautiful ancient Egyptian royal tombs. It is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Luxor. It is also known by several names, such as “Belzoni’s Cemetery” after its discoverer, the Italian explorer Giovanni Belzoni, as well as “Apis’ Cemetery” and “Psamis Ibn Necho’s Cemetery” in some ancient sources. The cemetery represents the final resting place of King Seti I, the second king of the Nineteenth Dynasty of the New Kingdom.

title: KV-3
description: Cemetery 3, known internationally as KV3, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is the tomb of one of the sons of the Egyptian Pharaoh Ramses III in the early Twentieth Dynasty. The “straight axis” design was followed in the construction of the tomb, which is the typical design followed in the construction of Twentieth Dynasty tombs. A sherd was found inside the tomb dating back to the twenty-eighth year of the reign of Ramesses III, engraved in hieratic script.

title: KV-4
description: Cemetery 4, known internationally as KV4, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It was built to be the final resting place of the Egyptian Pharaoh Ramesses Later, however, he abandoned the entire idea and was not buried in the cemetery either.

title: KV-46
description: Cemetery 46, known internationally as KV46, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is a non-royal cemetery belonging to a pair of nobles who lived through the rule of the Eighteenth Dynasty, namely Yuya and Tuyo. Parents of Queen Tiye, wife of Amenhotep III, and grandparents of Queen Nefertiti; Their tomb was discovered by James Edward Coybell, who was working in the Valley of the Kings under the absolute right of excavation and discovery granted by the Egyptian authorities to Theodoro Davis in February 1905, although Davis announced the discovery of the tomb two years after this date. It was the greatest archaeological discovery until the discovery of Tutankhamun.

title: KV47
description: Cemetery No. 47, known scientifically as KV47, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. The Pharaoh Siptah of the Nineteenth Dynasty was buried there, although a mummy of Siptah was found in Cemetery 35. The tomb was discovered by Edward R. Ayrton on 18 December 1905. Theodore M. Davis, Ayrton's financier, published an account of the site's discovery and excavations in 1908.

title: KV11
description: Cemetery 11, known internationally as KV11, is the royal tomb of Pharaoh Ramses III of Egypt, the second king of the Twentieth Dynasty. The cemetery is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings. Work began on it on orders from King Setnect, then work on it was stopped after excavation led to a breach in King Amenemse’s tomb. Setnect was then buried in Cemetery 14. With Ramesses III’s accession to the throne of Egypt, the excavation of the tomb was completed, but through another design axis to overflow. Other damage occurred to the tomb of King Amun Messes.

title: KV16
description: Cemetery No. 16, known scientifically as KV16, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt, and contains the burial of Pharaoh Ramesses I of the Nineteenth Dynasty. Its location was discovered by Giovanni Belzoni in October 1817.

title: KV9
description: Cemetery 9, known internationally as KV9, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It was built by Pharaoh Ramesses V to be his final resting place, but it was reused by his uncle Ramesses VI, who was buried there at a later period.

title: KV6
description: Cemetery 6, known internationally as KV6, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is the final resting place of Egyptian Pharaoh Ramesses IX, the eighth king of the Twentieth Dynasty. One of the distinctive features of this tomb is that work on it was not finished with the death of the king, as the features of the rush to finish the work appear clear, especially in the way the inscriptions were completed or the way the corners of the tomb were cut. It is also distinguished by its entrance being somewhat higher above the surface of the ground compared to the entrances of the two tombs surrounding it, in addition to the use of black colors. The inscriptions on the walls are dominated by dark blue and yellow, which is also unusual in the tombs of the Valley of the Kings.

title: KV5
description: Cemetery 5, known internationally as KV5, is located in the Eastern Valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is the largest tomb ever in the Valley of the Kings, as it extends 443.2 meters long and covers an area of ​​1,266.47 square metres. It belongs to the sons of Ramesses II, and work on it is still ongoing. Its discovery dates back to the year 1825, but it was not fully revealed except through the Theban Planning Project led by Kent Weeks in 1987.

title: KV7
description: Cemetery 7, known internationally as KV7, is located in the Valley of the Kings and is the final resting place of the ancient Egyptian Pharaoh Ramesses II, known as the third king of the Nineteenth Dynasty. It is located in the main valley in front of Cemetery 5, which includes his sons, and near the tomb of his son and successor, Merneptah. The tomb site is believed to have been severely damaged as a result of the annual Nile floods.

title: KV21
description: Cemetery 21, known internationally as Cemetery KV21, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings, Egypt. Discovered in 1817 by Giovanni Battista Belzoni, it contained the mummies of two women believed to be queens of the Eighteenth Dynasty.

title: KV28
description: Cemetery 28 is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in the Theban Cemetery in Upper Egypt. It consists of a short well leading to one rectangular room. The cemetery has been known since the 1830s and was mentioned by John Gardiner Wilkinson. In 1889, Eugène Lefebure said it contained parts of mummies and their casings. The tomb was excavated in the 1990s by Donald B. Rayyan, who found the bones of three individuals, fragments of a limestone canopic jar, several wooden pieces, and pottery dating back to the early and middle Eighteenth Dynasty. Its original owner was likely a nobleman, given the tomb's proximity to the tomb of Tuthmosis IV.

title: KV44
description: Tomb No. 44, known scientifically as KV44, is one of the tombs located in the Valley of the Kings in southern Egypt. It was discovered and excavated by English archaeologist Howard Carter in 1901 and re-examined in the 1990s by American archaeologist Donald Ryan. This tomb consists of one room connected by a vestibule or an external corridor dug into the rock. When the tomb was discovered, it was closed with rocks, and inside it, three mummies were discovered in wooden coffins. They were mummies: Tenterar, a housewife from the reign of King Osorkon I, Hoeva, and a singer of Amun whose name was not revealed. These burials, which belong to the Twenty-Second Dynasty, are clearly secondary burials as the coffins were placed on rubble that filled about a fifth of the volume of the tomb. In these ruins, the remains of seven mummies that preceded this era were found without coffins or funerary equipment. Numerous bee nests on the ceiling indicate that the tomb may have remained open for some time in ancient times. The original cut of the tomb dates back to the Eighteenth Dynasty. Nothing is known about the original owner of the original tomb, but it has been suggested that this was an unused tomb belonging to Queen Tiye's brother.

title: KV45
description: Cemetery No. 45, scientifically known by the symbol KV45, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is the cemetery of Serhat, the holder of the title overseeing the fields of Amun, and it dates back to the Eighteenth Dynasty.

title: KV8
description: Cemetery 8 is located in the Valley of the Kings in southern Egypt. It is the tomb of Pharaoh Merneptah from the Nineteenth Dynasty.

title: KV2
description: The Tomb of Ramses IV, or Tomb 2, known internationally as KV2, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt, specifically at the bottom of the eastern valley between Tomb 7 and Tomb 1. It is the royal tomb of Pharaoh Ramesses IV, the third king of the Twentieth Dynasty. The tomb has been open since ancient times, and many inscriptions in different languages ​​were found inside it, left by visitors to the tomb.

title: KV57
description: Cemetery 57, known internationally as KV57, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt and belongs to Pharaoh Horemheb, the last king of the Eighteenth Dynasty.

title: KV56
description: Cemetery No. 56, known scientifically as KV56, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. Known as the “Cemetery of Gold,” it was discovered by Egyptologist Edward Ayrton in January 1908. It contained what is believed to be the complete body of a royal child from the late Nineteenth Dynasty. The tomb and sarcophagus had decomposed. The figure was covered with a 1 cm thick layer of gold leaf and plaster around the original site. A pair of small silver gloves, a pair of silver bracelets with the names of Seti II and Tusret written on them, and a set of gold earrings bearing the name of Seti II were also found. It is not known who this cemetery belongs to.

title: KV49
description: Cemetery No. 49, known scientifically as KV49, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is a typical tomb from the Eighteenth Dynasty. It may have been used to restore mummies later in the New Kingdom.

title: KV-12
description: Cemetery No. 12, scientifically known by the symbol KV12, is an unusual cemetery. It was originally used during the Eighteenth Dynasty in ancient Egypt, then used again during the Nineteenth and Twentieth Dynasties, and it was likely that it was used to bury multiple members of the royal family, such as Cemetery No. 5.

title: KV48
description: Cemetery No. 48, scientifically known by the symbol KV48, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It contained the burial place of the nobleman Amun im Opet called Peri.

title: KV10
description: Amen Musa Cemetery or Cemetery 10 in the Valley of the Kings; The scientific designation of the tomb is KV10. It was believed that it was a tomb built for Pharaoh Amenmese of the Nineteenth Dynasty. But there are no traces indicating that he was actually buried there.

title: KV14
description: Cemetery 14, or the Cemetery of Teusert, known internationally as KV14, is a shared tomb that originally belonged to Queen Teusert, the last pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty known so far. It was then expanded and reused by Pharaoh Setnect, the first king of the Twentieth Dynasty. It has been open since ancient times, but it was not recorded and studied accurately except by the German Hartwig Altenmüller, who was sent by the University of Hamburg to study the cemetery in the period between 1983 and 1987.

title: KV61
description: Cemetery No. 61, known scientifically as KV61, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. When discovered, it appeared to be unused and unadorned, so the identity of those buried in it is unknown. Assuming that it was used, it seems that what was buried in it was later moved to another place.

title: KV15
description: Cemetery No. 15, known scientifically as KV15, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt, where King Seti II of the Nineteenth Dynasty was buried. The tomb was dug at the base of a near-vertical cliff at the head of a valley running southwest of the main part of the Valley of the Kings. It extends along an axis from northwest to southeast, and has a short entrance and then three corridors that end in the unexcavated well room. The well room is connected to a hall with four columns and another corridor that was used as a burial chamber.

title: KV34
description:
The tomb of Thutmose III, or with the scientific symbol KV34, is a rock-cut tomb of one of the Pharaohs of Egypt, Thutmose III. It is considered one of the first tombs of the kings of ancient Egypt in the Valley of the Kings in the western region of the Nile facing Thebes. Thutmose III belonged to the Eighteenth Dynasty during the New Kingdom of Egypt. This cemetery is distinguished by the beauty of its coordination and the precision of its design and implementation. Its entrance is a long, slanted underground corridor followed by a vertical hole - perhaps to hinder thieves - then slanted corridors and stairs leading to a high chamber, then stairs to a wide lower chamber, which is the coffin pit.
The rooms are engraved with drawings expressing the religious perception of the ancient Egyptians, and texts written in hieroglyphics from the Book of the Dead.

title: KV39
description: Tomb No. 39, known scientifically as KV39, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt, and is one of the possible sites for the tomb of King Amenhotep I. It is located high in the rocky cliffs, far from the bottom of the main valley, which contains most of the royal tombs. It is located in a small valley extending from the eastern side of the Horn Peak, directly under the hills where the workers' village is located.

title: KV30
description: Cemetery No. 30, known scientifically as KV30, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It was discovered by Belzoni in 1817, with funding from the 2nd Earl of Belmore. Therefore it is also known as “Lord Belmore’s Cemetery”.

title: KV31
description:
Cemetery No. 31, known scientifically as KV31, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. During the excavation seasons of 2010-2012, the tomb was examined within the “Valley of the Kings Project at the University of Basel,” where a map of the tomb was drawn for the first time. The tomb consists of a pillar (A), a room (B), and two additional rooms that can be accessed from room (B). Inside the tomb they found five mummies, two women and three males, their ages ranging between 18 and 30 years. Because the names of the mummies were not found, the mummies were attributed to the rooms in which they were found. Mummy Part 1 is female, 18-25 years old, with short, black hair like silk. 159 cm 
Mummy C2 is likely a male with long braided hair, between 20 and 25 years old. 165 cm (5'4)
Mummy C3 is most likely male. His body was found decapitated, with his arms folded across his chest in the style of a king. He was 18-25 years old. 175 cm (5'8)
The Mummy, Part 4, male. His hair was short except for long strands on the right side which suggest the lock of Horus. 160 cm, no age given, but back molars have appeared in the jaw.
It is possible that mummy D4 was female, but without confirmation. Only most of her skull, one leg, and part of her pelvis remained. She is approximately 155 cm tall, and is between 20 and 30 years old based on her teeth. Her hair was short and red.

title: KV52
description: Cemetery No. 52, known scientifically as KV52, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. A mummified monkey was discovered in it, and it is likely linked to the nearby tomb of Amenhotep II.

title: KV53
description: Cemetery No. 53, known scientifically as KV53, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is not fully planned, but consists of a single room at the end of a vertical corridor.

title: KV52
description: Cemetery No. 52, known scientifically as KV52, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. A mummified monkey was discovered in it, and it is likely linked to the nearby tomb of Amenhotep II.

title: KV37
description: Cemetery No. 37, known scientifically as KV37, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. Bone fragments indicate that the grave was used for burial, but their crushing makes it difficult to determine who these bones belong to and thus difficult to determine the identity of those buried in the cemetery.

title: KV36
description: Cemetery No. 36, known scientifically as KV36, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It contains the burial site of the noble Maherbari of the Eighteenth Dynasty.

title: KV58
description: Cemetery 58, known internationally as KV58, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is also known as the “Cemetery of the Military Chariot” not for the discovery of a war chariot there, but for the discovery of gold flakes bearing the names of Tutankhamun and Kheper-Kheperu-Ra-i, and it is believed that they are among the gold flakes that covered the royal war chariots at that time.

title: KV19
description: Cemetery 19, known internationally as KV19, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is the final resting place of Prince Mentuherkhepshef, the eldest son of Ramses IX. Studies indicate that the tomb was originally prepared for Prince Setharkhepshef, who was later known as Pharaoh Ramesses VIII. It was then used to bury Prince Mentuherkhepshef after his death during the era of his brother Ramesses X, while no evidence has yet been made of the personal tomb of Ramesses VIII.

title: KV43
description: Cemetery 43, known internationally as KV43, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is the tomb of the Egyptian Pharaoh Thutmose IV, the eighth king of the Eighteenth Dynasty. The tomb was discovered by Howard Carter, who led a scouting campaign at that time for the benefit of Theodore Davis, who in turn published a detailed note on the discovery of the tomb in 1904.

title: KV27
description: Cemetery 27 is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. This cemetery was visited by John Wilkinson, but was not fully explored until the 1990s by Donald B. Ryan from Pacific Lutheran University. The tomb consists of four rooms and is not decorated. Nothing is known about its owner.

title: KV20
description: Cemetery 20, known internationally as Cemetery KV20, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is likely that it is the first royal tomb built in the Valley of the Kings. It was originally built to be the final resting place for Egyptian Pharaoh Thutmose I. It was then used to bury Queen Hatshepsut, who expanded the cemetery to include her remains and those of her father side by side. The scholars of the French expedition were aware of the existence of the cemetery when they visited the area in 1799 and recorded it in Their scientific records were later published under the name Description of Egypt. However, the cemetery was not fully studied except by Howard Carter in 1903, despite the fact that many explorers flocked to it between 1799 and 1903. Tomb 20 is considered a unique model among all the tombs of the Valley of the Kings because of its unique design and its circular corridors for a distance of approximately 210 meters in a clockwise direction.

title: KV40
description: Cemetery No. 40, scientifically referred to as KV40, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. The original owner of this cemetery is unknown. Only the upper part of the vestibule or entrance to the tomb is accessible, the rest of the tomb is blocked off completely by rubble and pieces of stone, and nothing is known about the complete layout of the tomb. Although excavations were conducted in this cemetery by the French Egyptologist Victor Loret in 1899, no reports were published about it.

title: KV26
description: Tomb No. 26 is an ancient Egyptian tomb from the Eighteenth Dynasty, located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. The cemetery is located in a side valley that leads to the tomb of Tuthmosis III. It was visited by the early Egyptologist James Burton in the 1820s or 1830s, and by Victor Loret in 1898. It was mapped in the 1980s by the Thebes Map Project. The first documentation of excavations in the tomb was made in 2009 by the Valley of the Kings Project of the University of Basel. The tomb contained evidence of at least one burial, pottery fragments and stone vessels from the mid-Eighteenth Dynasty, but nothing is known about its occupant(s).

title: KV42
description: Cemetery 42, known internationally as KV42, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. The tomb was built for Queen Hatshepsut Meret Ra, the wife of Pharaoh Thutmose III, the sixth king of the Eighteenth Dynasty, and the mother of Pharaoh Amenhotep II, the seventh king of the Eighteenth Dynasty. However, she was never buried in this cemetery and it is likely that she was buried in her son’s tomb. Queen Hatshepsut Meret Ra is not related to Queen Hatshepsut V. Pharaohs of the Eighteenth Dynasty.

title: KV35
description: The Tomb of Amenhotep II or Tomb 35, known internationally as KV35, is in the Valley of the Kings, on the western bank of the Nile opposite the city of Luxor, Egypt. It is the final resting place of the Egyptian Pharaoh Amenhotep II, the sixth king of the Eighteenth Dynasty. The cemetery is distinguished by many architectural features that have not been seen before in cemeteries of that time period, including: The presence of a side chamber attached to the well chamber, and the presence of a passage between the descending stairs towards the burial chamber and the burial chamber itself. The design of the burial chamber is completely different from the design of the burial chambers in the tombs of the Eighteenth Dynasty, in which it was customary for the chamber to be cartouche-shaped, while the burial chamber in the tomb was rectangular in shape and built on two levels, a design that was later followed in the tombs of the Nineteenth Dynasty.

title: WV23
description: Tomb 23, known internationally as WV23, is located in the Western Valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is the final resting place of the Egyptian Pharaoh Kheperheperure, the thirteenth king of the Eighteenth Dynasty. It was discovered by the Italian Egyptologist Giovanni Battista Belzoni during the winter of 1816. It is completely similar in its interior design to the tomb believed to be that of Akhenaten, in terms of the descending corridor devoid of inscriptions leading to the well chamber, which has no inscriptions. It also contains an opening overlooking the surface of the earth, through which the passage leads to the burial chamber, where the king’s stone coffin is located.

title: Child Museum
description: The Child Museum is a well-known museum located in Egypt. It is a popular destination for locals and tourists alike.

title: Sound & Light Show
description: The Sound & Light Show is a well-known attraction located in Egypt. It is a popular destination for locals and tourists alike.

title: KV38
description: Tomb 38, known internationally as KV38, is located in the eastern valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It is the tomb that Thutmose III ordered to be built in honor of the memory of his grandfather Thutmose I, the third king of the Eighteenth Dynasty. After its completion, he moved his grandfather’s royal coffin from Tomb 20 and placed it in a new coffin that he designed specifically for him, other than the coffin that contained the coffin in the previous tomb.

title: KV13
description: Tomb No. 13, known scientifically as KV13, is located in the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. It was originally excavated and inscribed for the burial of the noble Bey from the late Nineteenth Dynasty. The French Journal of Egyptology (BIFAO) published in 2000 an inscribed fragment stating that the advisor Bey had been executed by King Siptah. Consequently, Pi was never buried in his tomb. Moreover, no funerary furniture belonging to Bai was found in this tomb. It was later reused to bury Prince Amun Harkhepshef and again to bury Prince Mentuharkhepshef, both from the Twentieth Dynasty.

title: WV25
description: Cemetery 25, known internationally as WV25, is an unfinished cemetery located in the Western Valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. The cemetery bears the characteristics of royal tombs, except that it is completely devoid of any decorations or inscriptions, as it was never completed in any subsequent period of time. It is likely that it was the tomb that was prepared for Akhenaten before he moved the capital of his kingdom from Thebes to Akheten and built his own funerary city there.

title: WV24
description: Cemetery 24, known internationally as Cemetery WV24, is an ancient Egyptian cemetery located in the Valley of the Kings, Egypt. The tomb does not appear to have buried members of the Eighteenth Dynasty. However, it was later used in the Third Intermediate Period to bury at least five individuals, including an infant.

title: VW22
description: Cemetery 22, known internationally as WV22, is located in the Western Valley of the Valley of the Kings in Egypt. The cemetery is distinguished by being the final resting place of one of the greatest pharaohs of the New Kingdom, Amenhotep III, in addition to the presence of two burial chambers attached to the cemetery belonging to the two wives of Amenhotep III. Queen Tiye and Princess Set-Amun. Otherwise, the tomb is the largest of the Western Valley tombs discovered so far. The interior design of the tomb and the style of engraving and decoration in it are in line with the tombs of Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV, the predecessors of Amenhotep III. However, this tomb is distinguished by the quality of the inscriptions, unlike its two predecessors.

title: WVA
description: WVA, also known as KV A, is a small single room tomb in the Western Valley of the Kings associated with WV22, the tomb of Pharaoh Amenhotep III of the Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt. Located 60 metres (200 ft) south of the tomb of Amenhotep III, it was discovered by Karl Richard Lepsius in 1845; he recorded that it contained pottery bearing the name of a king. The tomb was re-excavated in the 1990s by a team from Waseda University led by Sakuji Yoshimura and Jiro Kondo. They found the tomb contained assorted jars and sealings, indicating the tomb was likely used as storage for overflow from the nearby tomb of Amenhotep III.

title: Headless Pyramid
description: The Headless Pyramid, otherwise identified as Lepsius XXIX or Steinpyramide XXIX, is the remain of a pyramid complex built in Saqqara. The identity of the pyramid owner is unclear, though it is suspected to belong to either pharaoh Menkauhor of the Fifth Dynasty or pharaoh Merikare of the Tenth Dynasty, both of whom are known to have built a pyramid. If associated with Menkauhor, the pyramid's name is either Nṯr-ỉswt Mn-kꜣw-ḥr meaning 'Divine are the places of Menkauhor' or Nṯr-ỉswt Ỉkꜣw-Ḥr meaning 'Divine are the places of Ikauhor' referencing Menkauhor's birthname; if associated with Merikare, the pyramid's name is Wꜣḏ-swt Mry-kꜣ-rꜥ meaning 'Fresh are the places of Merikare'. Other candidates for the pyramid owner that have been proposed are Amenemhat I of the Twelfth Dynasty and an ephemeral pharaoh Ity of the Eighth Dynasty.

title: Al-Fattah Al-Aleem Mosque
description: Al-Fattah Al-Aleem Mosque is one of the mosques in the New Administrative Capital in Egypt with a distinctive, modern Islamic architectural style. The mosque is located at the entrance to the Administrative Capital on the Central Ring Road. It was opened on January 6, 2019 at the same time as the opening of the Cathedral of the Nativity of Christ, which is the largest cathedral in the Middle East and is located in the same city.

title: Arena Theatre
description: The Arena Theatre is a well-known theatre located in Egypt. It is a popular destination for locals and tourists alike.

title: Qani Bey Mosque
description: The Mosque of Qani-Bay is a mosque near the Salah al-Din Square in Islamic Cairo, Egypt. The complex is named after Qani-Bay al-Sayfi, nicknamed "al-Rammah", who was Grand Master of the Horse during the reign of Sultan al-Ghuri.

title: Kekhya Mosque
description: Othman Katkhuda Al-Qazdaghli Mosque, or Al-Kikhia Mosque, is one of the mosques established in the era of the Ottoman Empire in Egypt. This mosque is located in the Azbakeya neighborhood at the intersection of Ibrahim Street and Qasr Al-Nil Street.

title: Palace of Culture
description: The Palace of Culture is a well-known theatre located in Egypt. It is a popular destination for locals and tourists alike.

title: Kom el-Nana
description: Kom el-Nana is an archaeological site near the ancient Egyptian city of Akhet-Aten. It lies south of the city and east of the modern village of el-Hagg Quandil. For a long time its ruins were thought to be those of a Roman military camp, but between 1988 and 2000 Barry Kemp excavated remains of an Amarna period stone temple with garden and subsidiary buildings including a bakery and a brewery. Neither the original name nor the owner of the complex has been identified. It is likely to have been a sun temple and is very similar to Maru-Aten. It consists of a brick enclosure with an area of 228×213 m; it is divided into two unequal parts by an east-west wall. It is likely that pylon gates opened on all four outer walls. Since it stood at a very prominent place – at the southern end of the so-called Royal Road, the main street of Akhet-Aten – it's possibly identical with the sunshade temple of Nefertiti mentioned on the boundary stelae.

title: Maadi Public Library
description: The Maadi Public Library is a well-known library located in Egypt. It is a popular destination for locals and tourists alike.

title: Ras El Tin Palace
description: Ras El Tin Palace is a palace on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea in Alexandria, Egypt. It is one of the official residences for a serving President of Egypt. title: El-Lahuun

description: Cemetery 55, known internationally as KV55, is located in the Eastern Valley in the Valley of the Kings in Upper Egypt. Since the discovery of the tomb, it has been believed that the mummy that was found is that of the Pharaoh Akhenaten. This was confirmed by genetic tests and laboratory research conducted on the mummy. These tests were announced in February 2010 and revealed that the owner of the tomb was the son of Amenhotep III and at the same time the father of Tutankhamun. In addition, the age of the mummy's owner is consistent with Akhenaten's age at his death. This leaves no room for doubt that the mummy that was found is actually the mummy of Akhenaten.

title: Nefertari-Merymut tomb
description: QV66 is the tomb of Nefertari, the Great Wife of Pharaoh Ramesses II, in Egypt's Valley of the Queens. It was discovered by Ernesto Schiaparelli in 1904. Nefertari, which means "The most beautiful (one) among them", was Ramesses II's favorite wife; he went out of his way to make this obvious, referring to her as "the one for whom the sun shines" in his writings, built the Temple of Hathor at Abu Simbel to idolize her as a deity, and commissioned portraiture wall paintings. In the Valley of the Queens, Nefertari's tomb once held the mummified body and representative symbolisms of her, consistent with most Egyptian tombs of the period. Now, everything has been looted except for two thirds of the 5,200 square feet of wall paintings. For what still remains, these wall paintings characterized Nefertari's character. Her face received particular attention to emphasize her beauty, especially the shape of her eyes, the blush of her cheeks, and her eyebrows. Some paintings were full of lines and color of red, blue, yellow, and green that portrayed exquisite directions to navigating through the afterlife to paradise.

description: The tomb of Tutankhamun, a pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty of ancient Egypt, is located in the Valley of the Kings. The tomb, also known by its tomb number KV62, consists of four chambers and an entrance staircase and corridor. It is smaller and less extensively decorated than other Egyptian royal tombs of its time, and it probably originated as a tomb for a non-royal individual that was adapted for Tutankhamun's use after his premature death. Like other pharaohs, Tutankhamun was buried with a wide variety of funerary objects and personal possessions, such as coffins, furniture, clothing and jewelry, though in the unusually limited space these goods had to be densely packed. Robbers entered the tomb twice in the years immediately following the burial, but Tutankhamun's mummy and most of the burial goods remained intact. The tomb's low position, dug into the floor of the valley, allowed its entrance to be hidden by debris deposited by flooding and tomb construction. Thus, unlike other tombs in the valley, it was not stripped of its valuables during the Third Intermediate Period.

Because of Montu's strong association with raging bulls, the temple was a major center of worship for bulls, containing many statues of bulls for worship and reliefs. description: The Muhammad Ali Mosque, also known as the Mosque of Muhammad Ali, is a mosque located in the Citadel of Cairo, Egypt. It was commissioned by Muhammad Ali Pasha and built between 1832 and 1857. Overlooking the city, it is one of the most visible mosques and landmarks in the skyline of Cairo. Unlike the traditional Cairene architecture that preceded it, the mosque was built in an entirely Ottoman and European-influenced style, further setting it apart from other monuments. It is sometimes called the Alabaster Mosque due to the prominent use of alabaster as a covering for its walls.

title: Mosque Of Al Nasser Mohammad Ibn Qalaun
description: The Al-Nasir Muhammad Mosque, or more formally, the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun Mosque, is a mosque located in the Citadel of Cairo, Egypt. Completed in 1318 CE, the mosque was built by the Mamluk sultan Al-Nasr Muhammad as the royal mosque of the Citadel, where the sultans of Cairo performed their Friday prayers. The mosque is located across the street from the courtyard access to the Mosque of Muhammad Ali. The Sultan also built a religious complex in the center of the city, adjacent to the one by his father Qalawun.

title: Giza Zoo
description: The Giza Zoo is a zoological garden in Giza, Egypt. It is one of the few green areas in the city, and includes Giza's largest park. The zoo covers about 80 acres (32 ha), and is home to many endangered species, as well as a selection of endemic fauna.

title: Temple of Horus
description: The Temple of Edfu is an Egyptian temple located on the west bank of the Nile in Edfu, Upper Egypt. The city was known in the Hellenistic period in Koine Greek as Ἀπόλλωνος πόλις and in Latin as Apollonopolis Magna, after the chief god Horus, who was identified as Apollo under the interpretatio graeca. It is one of the best preserved shrines in Egypt. The temple was built in the Ptolemaic Kingdom between 237 and 57 BC. The inscriptions on its walls provide important information on language, myth and religion during the Hellenistic period in Egypt. In particular, the Temple's inscribed building texts "provide details [both] of its construction, and also preserve information about the mythical interpretation of this and all other temples as the Island of Creation." There are also "important scenes and inscriptions of the Sacred Drama which related the age-old conflict between Horus and Seth." They are translated by the Edfu-Project.

title: Karnak Temple Complex
description: The Karnak Temple Complex, commonly known as Karnak, comprises a vast mix of temples, pylons, chapels, and other buildings near Luxor, Egypt. Construction at the complex began during the reign of Senusret I in the Middle Kingdom and continued into the Ptolemaic Kingdom, although most of the extant buildings date from the New Kingdom. The area around Karnak was the ancient Egyptian Ipet-isut and the main place of worship of the 18th Dynastic Theban Triad, with the god Amun as its head.

title: Wadi es-Sebua Temple
description: Wadi Al-Seboua or Wadi Al-Aswad is the site of two modern Egyptian temples. The first temple was built by the Eighteenth Dynasty pharaoh Amenhotep III and was later restored by Ramesses II. In its first phase, the temple consisted of a rock shelter in front of a brick edifice, a hall and a hall partly painted with frescoes. The temple was probably dedicated to a local Nubian form of Horus, but was changed to Amun later. During the Amarna period, images of Amun were attacked and the decorations deteriorated. The second temple was built by the Nineteenth Dynasty Pharaoh Ramesses II in Lower Nubia. He rebuilt and expanded the Temple of Amenhotep III by building structures in front of the edifice.

title: Bubastis
description: Bubastis, also known in Arabic as Tell-Basta or in Egyptian as Per-Bast, was an ancient Egyptian city. Bubastis is often identified with the biblical Pi-Beseth. It was the capital of its own nome, located along the River Nile in the Delta region of Lower Egypt, and notable as a center of worship for the feline goddess Bastet, and therefore the principal depository in Egypt of mummies of cats.

title: Grand Egyptian Museum
description: The Grand Egyptian Museum is an archaeological and national museum located about 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) from the Giza Pyramid Complex, in Giza, Egypt. Dedicated to Ancient Egypt and its culture, society, and artifacts, it is the largest museum in the world for a single civilization.

title: Madrasa and Khanqa of Sultan Barquq
description: The Mosque-Madrasa of Sultan Barquq, also known as the Mosque-Madrasa-Khanqah of Az-Zaher Barquq, is a religious complex situated in the Bayn al-Qasrayn area of Al-Mu'izz Street, in Islamic Cairo, Egypt. The complex was commissioned by Sultan al-Zahir Barquq as a school for religious education in the four Islamic schools of thought, composed of a mosque, madrasa, mausoleum, and khanqah.

title: Sulayman Pasha Mosque
description: The Sulayman Pasha Mosque, also known as the Sulayman Pasha al-Khadem Mosque, and as the Sariat al-Jabal Mosque, is a mosque, mausoleum and shrine, located inside the Citadel at the top of Mount Mokattam, in Islamic Cairo, Egypt. The mosque was completed in 1528 CE by Suleiman Pasha Al-Khadem, one of the Ottoman-era rulers of Egypt. It was originally erected for the use of the janissaries stationed in the northern enclosure. It is the first mosque established in Egypt in Ottoman architectural style.

title: Madrasa of Sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad Ibn Qalawun
description: The Madrasa of al-Nasir Muhammad is a madrasa and mausoleum located in the Bayn al-Qasrayn area of al-Muizz street in Islamic Cairo, Egypt. It was built in the name of the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, but its construction began between 1294 and 1295 under the reign of Sultan al-Adil Kitbugha, who was sultan in between al-Nasir Muhammad's first and seconds reigns. When al-Nasir Muhammad returned to the throne in 1299 he oversaw its construction until its completion in 1303. It is located adjacent to the earlier Qalawun complex, and the later Madrasa of Sultan Barquq.

title: Nefertari's Temple of Hathor
description: El Templo de Nefertari, también conocido como "Templo de Hathor", fue construido bajo el mandato del tercer faraón egipcio de la Dinastía XIX, Ramsés II, como homenaje a su esposa, la reina Nefertari, siendo unos de los escasos ejemplos de grandes templos dedicados a una mujer en el Antiguo Egipto y que forma parte, junto con el Templo de Ramsés II, del complejo de Abu Simbel.
